body:
Prehistoric Gujarat Beyond Langhnaj

Although Langhnaj is a particularly well-known Mesolithic site, prehistoric evidence is distributed across several regions of Gujarat.

The archaeological record includes older Palaeolithic stone-tool sites in eastern Gujarat, microlithic settlements in North Gujarat and locations where later pottery-using and food-producing communities occupied areas previously used by hunter-gatherers.

This distribution is important because it demonstrates that Gujarat's prehistoric development cannot be explained by a single site or a single pattern of settlement.

Important Sites and Their Associations

SiteLocationMain association
LanghnajMehsana districtMicroliths, human remains and wild animal bones
LoteshwarSami area, Patan districtEarly Mesolithic occupation followed by Chalcolithic occupation
Santhli or SanthaliNorth GujaratEarly microlith-using hunter-gatherers and wild animal remains
Vaharvo TimboNorth GujaratPrehistoric occupation investigated through the North Gujarat Archaeological Project
DatranaNorth GujaratImportant archaeological locality investigated by the North Gujarat Archaeological Project
Jogpura and BhuveraEastern GujaratPalaeolithic stone-tool assemblages, including Middle Palaeolithic evidence

Loteshwar: An Important Site in Patan District

Loteshwar is located in the Sami area of present-day Patan district, North Gujarat. It is especially important because archaeological investigations identified remains belonging to different periods.

Its early occupation is associated with Mesolithic hunter-gatherers who used microliths. Evidence includes small stone tools and animal remains. Wild animals, particularly blackbuck, formed an important part of the recorded fauna.

Published archaeological studies place early microlithic occupations at Loteshwar and nearby Santhli broadly within approximately 7100–5600 BCE. These are regional archaeological estimates and should not be treated as exact dates for every Mesolithic settlement in Gujarat.

A later occupation at Loteshwar belongs to the Chalcolithic period and is commonly placed around 3600–3000 BCE. It includes pottery and evidence associated with communities whose economy involved animal exploitation and developing food production.

Loteshwar has evidence of more than one cultural period. Its earlier Mesolithic occupation must be distinguished from its later Chalcolithic occupation.

Santhli: Early Hunter-Gatherer Evidence

Santhli, also written as Santhali in archaeological publications, is another important early microlithic locality of North Gujarat.

Its early deposits are associated with hunter-gatherers who exploited wild animals. Research has particularly associated the site with wild buffalo remains.

The significance of Santhli is that it provides evidence of an early microlithic occupation alongside the wider prehistoric sequence represented at Loteshwar.

Other Mesolithic Localities

Additional excavated Mesolithic localities recorded in Gujarat include Akhaj, Valasana and Hirpura. These names demonstrate that Mesolithic evidence extends beyond Langhnaj.

Prehistoric studies of the Sabarmati region also identify a broader distribution of microlithic settlements in North Gujarat. The association of these communities with sandy surfaces and nearby water sources is an important regional characteristic.

Datrana and Vaharvo Timbo

Datrana and Vaharvo Timbo are among the sites investigated through the North Gujarat Archaeological Project, a collaborative research initiative involving the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda and research institutions in Spain.

Investigations in this region have helped establish that prehistoric communities used North Gujarat's sandy landscapes over long periods. The regional evidence includes hunter-gatherer occupations and later communities associated with changing patterns of food production.

The presence of several prehistoric sites within the same region is consistent with repeated use of favourable landscapes, especially those offering water, wild animals and vegetation.

Older Palaeolithic Evidence in Eastern Gujarat

The prehistoric record of Gujarat extends back before the Mesolithic.

Stone-tool remains from the Orsang valley and other parts of eastern Gujarat include Palaeolithic industries. Research at Jogpura and Bhuvera has identified assemblages associated with Middle Palaeolithic technology.

These sites are important for distinguishing the older Palaeolithic occupation of Gujarat from the later microlithic hunter-gatherer communities represented by Langhnaj and Loteshwar.

Why the Regional Sequence Matters

The findings from these sites show that stone-tool technology continued to be important even while other aspects of daily life changed.

At some locations, microlithic hunter-gatherer remains occur below later deposits containing pottery and evidence of food-producing communities. This demonstrates a chronological sequence at the site, but it does not necessarily prove that the same population remained there continuously or that every change occurred in one generation.

Prelims focus

  • Loteshwar is located in the Sami area of Patan district, Gujarat.
  • Loteshwar has both Mesolithic and later Chalcolithic evidence.
  • Early microlithic occupations at Loteshwar and Santhli are reported from approximately 7100–5600 BCE.
  • The later Chalcolithic occupation at Loteshwar is commonly dated to approximately 3600–3000 BCE.
  • Akhaj, Valasana and Hirpura are among Gujarat's recorded Mesolithic localities.
  • Trap: The presence of a later Chalcolithic occupation at Loteshwar does not make its earlier Mesolithic deposits agricultural.

[Sources: Kuldeep K. Bhan, Review of Prehistoric Cultures of Gujarat and Need to Develop Accurate Settlement Gazetteer, sections Microlithic Settlements and Chalcolithic Settlements, printed pp. 328–330, consulted 17 November 2026; M. Madella and colleagues, Social and Environmental Transitions in Arid Zones: The North Gujarat Archaeological Project — NoGAP, Antiquity 84, 2010, sections Introduction and First Results, consulted 17 November 2026; Universitat Pompeu Fabra, North Gujarat Archaeological Project, project overview, consulted 17 November 2026; IGNOU, Indian Mesolithic Cultures, Unit 2, section 2.4, printed p. 20, consulted 17 November 2026; Gopesh Jha and colleagues, Assessing Systematic Blade Production in the Indian Subcontinent with Special Reference to Eastern Gujarat, Quaternary 6(2), 2023, article 25, sections 3.1 and 4.1, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Other Prehistoric Sites of Gujarat: From Palaeolithic Tools to Mesolithic Settlements

body:
From Collecting Food to Producing Food

For much of prehistory, people obtained food mainly by hunting wild animals, fishing and collecting naturally growing plants. Over time, some communities began deliberately growing plants and looking after animals.

This was an important change because people gradually gained greater control over certain sources of food.

The transition is often associated with the Neolithic period, but farming and herding did not begin simultaneously across the Indian subcontinent. Different regions developed different combinations of hunting, gathering, cultivation and animal husbandry.

What Is Domestication?

Domestication is the gradual process through which humans cultivate and manage plants or breed and manage animals, often selecting desirable characteristics over generations.

In plants, people could preserve seeds from useful varieties and deliberately sow them. In animals, they could protect, feed and breed selected individuals.

Gathering wild grain means collecting grain that grows naturally. Cultivating grain means deliberately growing and tending the plants. The distinction is essential because the discovery of wild seeds or grinding stones does not, by itself, demonstrate agriculture.

Similarly, finding the bones of cattle does not automatically establish cattle domestication. The animals may have been wild or domesticated, depending on the evidence from the particular site.

Why Farming and Herding Developed

Changes in climate, vegetation and animal populations influenced the development of food production.

As conditions became warmer after the last Ice Age, grasslands expanded in many regions. People encountered wild cereals and grazing animals more frequently. Their knowledge of plant growth and animal behaviour created opportunities for the gradual development of cultivation and herding.

People may have begun protecting useful plants, preserving their seeds and encouraging their growth. Animals that were relatively manageable could be kept near settlements, protected and eventually bred.

Domestication was not a single event. It developed over long periods through repeated human interaction with plants and animals.

How Food Production Changed Daily Life

More Regular Access to Food

Growing crops allowed communities to obtain food through planned cultivation rather than depending entirely on naturally available plants. Herding provided access to animal products such as meat and milk.

Food Storage

Harvested grains could be stored for later consumption or for use as seeds. Communities developed storage methods such as baskets, pits and clay containers.

Settlement Patterns

Cultivation often encouraged people to remain near fields while crops grew. More regular food supplies could support longer-lasting settlements and larger communities.

However, herding did not necessarily require permanent settlement. Pastoral communities could continue moving with their animals in search of grazing land and water.

Continued Hunting and Gathering

Food production did not immediately replace older activities. Farmers and herders might continue hunting, fishing and gathering wild plants. Other communities could remain primarily hunter-gatherers.

Early Farming and Herding in the Indian Subcontinent

NCERT identifies the northwestern part of the subcontinent as an important early region for the domestication of wheat, barley, sheep and goats.

Mehrgarh, located in present-day Pakistan near the Bolan Pass, is an important early farming and herding site. Settlement there began approximately 8,000 years ago according to the introductory NCERT framework.

Mehrgarh provides useful background for understanding the development of food production in northwestern South Asia. It must not be confused with a prehistoric site in Gujarat.

Evidence of Emerging Food Production in Gujarat

The archaeological record of North Gujarat provides evidence for a gradual change from hunter-gatherer economies to communities that used domesticated animals and, in some areas, cultivated plants.

Loteshwar and the Later Chalcolithic Period

Loteshwar is particularly useful because its earlier Mesolithic occupation can be distinguished from a later Chalcolithic occupation.

The later Chalcolithic evidence, commonly dated to around 3600–3000 BCE, includes pottery and material associated with communities whose economy combined different food resources.

Archaeological research indicates that domestic cattle were part of the economy of North Gujarat by the beginning of the 4th millennium BCE. This is important evidence for the development of animal husbandry in the region.

Research has also suggested the development of local cultivation involving small millets, including grasses belonging to groups such as Panicum and Setaria. The precise origins and extent of these early cultivation practices require qualification; they should not be treated as evidence that every community in North Gujarat practised agriculture at the same time.

Hunting, Herding and Farming Could Coexist

The shift towards food production was gradual rather than an immediate replacement of one way of life by another.

Some communities continued to use microliths while other communities made pottery, kept livestock and cultivated crops. At certain sites, different activities may have formed part of the same community's economy.

Three distinctions are particularly important:

  • Hunting is not herding: Hunting obtains animals from wild populations, while herding involves the management of livestock.
  • Gathering is not cultivation: Collecting wild plants differs from deliberately growing and tending crops.
  • Pastoralism is not necessarily settled agriculture: Herders may move seasonally even when other communities live near permanent fields.

Understanding Gujarat's Overall Prehistoric Development

The evidence from Gujarat demonstrates a long history of human adaptation to different environments.

Older Palaeolithic stone tools show early human activity in river valleys and rocky areas. The Mesolithic remains of Langhnaj and Loteshwar reveal the importance of hunting, gathering and small stone implements in North Gujarat. Later Chalcolithic evidence, including that from Loteshwar, demonstrates the increasing importance of pottery, livestock and developing food-production practices.

These developments did not create a single, uniform sequence followed by every community. Gujarat's prehistoric record instead shows regional variation and the continued use of older practices alongside newer ones.

Prelims focus

  • Domestication involves the gradual human management and breeding of plants or animals.
  • Mehrgarh is an important early farming site in present-day Pakistan, not Gujarat.
  • Loteshwar preserves earlier Mesolithic and later Chalcolithic evidence.
  • Domestic cattle were present in the economy of North Gujarat by the beginning of the 4th millennium BCE.
  • The transition to food production was gradual and varied between regions.
  • Trap: Pottery, grinding stones or cattle bones alone do not establish that a particular prehistoric community cultivated crops or domesticated animals.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, printed pp. 16–17, and Chapter 3, From Gathering to Growing Food, printed pp. 22–29; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 4, Timeline and Sources of History, printed pp. 70–73; M. Madella and colleagues, Social and Environmental Transitions in Arid Zones: The North Gujarat Archaeological Project — NoGAP, Antiquity 84, 2010, sections Introduction and First Results, consulted 17 November 2026; Kuldeep K. Bhan, Review of Prehistoric Cultures of Gujarat and Need to Develop Accurate Settlement Gazetteer, sections Microlithic Settlements and Chalcolithic Settlements, printed pp. 328–330, consulted 17 November 2026.]
